name: Chapter 13: Nuclei
description: Composition and size of the nucleus, mass defect and binding energy, nuclear force, radioactivity, fission and fusion

cards.term: How much smaller is the nucleus than the atom? Volume ratio?
cards.definition: Radius smaller by about 10⁴; volume about 10⁻¹² of the atom, yet it holds > 99.9% of the mass

cards.term: Analogy for atom vs nucleus size?
cards.definition: If the atom were a classroom, the nucleus would be a pinhead

cards.term: Define the atomic mass unit (u).
cards.definition: 1/12 of the mass of one ¹²C atom: 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV/c²

cards.term: Isotopes: definition and why they behave chemically alike?
cards.definition:
Atoms of the same element (same Z) with different mass (different N).
Identical electronic structure gives the same chemistry and the same place in the periodic table

cards.term: Why is chlorine’s atomic mass 35.46 u, not an integer?
cards.definition: Weighted average of isotopes: 75.4% × 34.98 + 24.6% × 36.98 = 35.47 u

cards.term: Isotopes of hydrogen?
cards.definition: Protium ¹H (99.985%), deuterium ²H, tritium ³H (unstable, artificial)

cards.term: Masses of proton, neutron and electron in u?
cards.definition: mp = 1.00727 u mn = 1.00866 u me = 0.00055 u (mH = 1.00783 u = mp + me)

cards.term: Mass of proton and neutron in kg?
cards.definition: mp = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; mn = 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg

cards.term: Why can’t electrons be inside the nucleus?
cards.definition: Ruled out by quantum theory arguments; all Z electrons are outside, and the nucleus has exactly Z protons

cards.term: Discovery of the neutron: who, when and how?
cards.definition: Chadwick, 1932: beryllium bombarded by α-particles emitted neutral radiation that knocked protons out of light nuclei; photons would need too much energy, so it was a new neutral particle. Nobel Prize 1935

cards.term: Free neutron vs bound neutron?
cards.definition: Free neutron is unstable (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄, mean life ≈ 1000 s); inside the nucleus it is stable

cards.term: Define Z, N and A.
cards.definition: Z = atomic number (protons) N = neutron number A = Z + N = mass number = number of nucleons

cards.term: Nuclide notation and example?
cards.definition: \( {}^{A}_{Z}X \): gold ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au has 79 protons and 118 neutrons

cards.term: Isotopes, isobars, isotones?
cards.definition: Isotopes: same Z (e.g. ¹H, ²H). Isobars: same A (³H and ³He). Isotones: same N (¹⁹⁸Hg and ¹⁹⁷Au)

cards.term: Mnemonic for isotopes / isobars / isotones?
cards.definition: Iso-TOPE = same TOP number (Z at the top of the periodic-table position) Iso-BAR = same “bulk” (A) Iso-TONE = same “n”umber of neutrons

cards.term: Teacher addition: ratio N/Z for stable nuclei?
cards.definition: ≈ 1 for light nuclei rising to about 1.5 for heavy nuclei (extra neutrons offset proton repulsion). Only ~10% of known isotopes are stable

cards.term: Teacher addition: electrons in a neutral atom vs nucleus for ²³⁸₉₂U?
cards.definition: Protons 92, neutrons 146, electrons 92 (neutral atom), nucleons 238

cards.term: How did α-scattering bound the nuclear size?
cards.definition:
A 5.5 MeV α-particle reaches a closest distance of about 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m from gold.
Rutherford’s Coulomb scattering held, so the nucleus is smaller than this

cards.term: Why use faster α-particles or electron beams?
cards.definition:
At higher energy the α gets closer and deviations from pure Coulomb scattering (short-range nuclear force) show up, revealing the size.
Fast electrons measure the charge distribution accurately

cards.term: Nuclear radius formula?
Why is the nuclear density independent of A?
cards.definition: Volume ∝ R³ ∝ A, and mass ∝ A, so density = constant (nuclei behave like drops of liquid of constant density)

cards.term: Nuclear density value and comparison?
cards.definition: About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, ~10¹⁴ times that of water; comparable to a neutron star

cards.term: Nuclear density of iron (Example 13.1)
cards.definition: ρ ≈ 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 13.1 · nuclear density

Find the missing step.

Iron nucleus: mass 55.85 u = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, A = 56. Find the nuclear density.
  1. R = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 56^{1/3} fm
  2. Volume = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π(1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³ × 56
  3. ρ = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁶ / [(4/3)π(1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³ × 56]
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 13.1 · nuclear density

Find the missing step.

Iron nucleus: mass 55.85 u = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, A = 56. Find the nuclear density.
  1. R = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 56^{1/3} fm
  2. Volume = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π(1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³ × 56
  3. ρ = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁶ / [(4/3)π(1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³ × 56]
  4. ρ ≈ 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³

cards.term: Exercise 13.4: ratio of the radii of ¹⁹⁷Au and ¹⁰⁷Ag?
cards.definition: R ∝ A1/3: (197/107)1/3 = 1.23

cards.term: Exercise 13.10: show that nuclear density is nearly constant.
cards.definition: ρ = mass/volume = A mp/[(4/3)π R₀³A] = 3mp/(4πR₀³), independent of A (≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³)

cards.term: Points to ponder: why does the radius from electron scattering differ slightly from the α-scattering value?
cards.definition: Electrons sense the charge distribution of the nucleus; α-particles and similar probes sense the nuclear matter

cards.term: Teacher addition: radius of ⁶⁴Cu vs ²⁷Al?
cards.definition: R ∝ A1/3: (64/27)1/3 = 1.33 (RCu = 4.8 fm, RAl = 3.6 fm)

cards.term: Einstein’s mass–energy equivalence?
cards.definition: \( E = mc^2 \); mass is another form of energy. So mass and energy are conserved together, not separately

cards.term: Example 13.2: energy equivalent of 1 g?
cards.definition: E = 10⁻³ × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹³ J

cards.term: Define mass defect.
cards.definition: \[\Delta M = [Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n] - M\]the constituent mass minus the actual nuclear mass (always positive)

cards.term: Binding energy in terms of mass defect?
cards.definition: \[E_b = \Delta M\,c^2\](energy needed to separate the nucleus into free nucleons; energy released when it forms)

cards.term: Energy equivalent of 1 u?
cards.definition: 931.5 MeV (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²; 1 u = 1.4924 × 10⁻¹⁰ J)

cards.term: Atomic vs nuclear masses in mass-defect problems: what should you do?
cards.definition:
Use atomic masses with mH for Z protons plus Z electrons:
ΔM = Z mH + (A − Z)mn − Matom
(electron masses cancel; ignore electron binding)

cards.term: Mass defect of oxygen-16 (Example 13.3)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 13.3 · oxygen-16

Find the missing step.

¹⁶₈O: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, atomic mass 15.99493 u. Find the mass defect and binding energy.
  1. Constituents: 8 × 1.00727 + 8 × 1.00866 = 16.12744 u (with 8 electrons: 16.13184 u)
  2. Nuclear mass = 15.99493 − 8 × 0.00055 = 15.99053 u
  3. ΔM = 16.12744 − 15.99053 = 0.13691 u
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 13.3 · oxygen-16

Find the missing step.

¹⁶₈O: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, atomic mass 15.99493 u. Find the mass defect and binding energy.
  1. Constituents: 8 × 1.00727 + 8 × 1.00866 = 16.12744 u (with 8 electrons: 16.13184 u)
  2. Nuclear mass = 15.99493 − 8 × 0.00055 = 15.99053 u
  3. ΔM = 16.12744 − 15.99053 = 0.13691 u
  4. E_b = 0.13691 × 931.5 = 127.5 MeV; per nucleon ≈ 7.97 MeV

cards.term: Define binding energy per nucleon.
cards.definition: \[E_{bn} = \dfrac{E_b}{A}\]the average energy per nucleon needed to remove all nucleons; a measure of stability

cards.term: Describe the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve.
cards.definition:
Rises steeply for light nuclei
Nearly flat (~8 MeV) for 30 < A < 170, with a peak 8.75–8.8 MeV at A = 56 (Fe)
Then falls slowly to 7.6 MeV at A = 238

cards.term: Which nucleus is the most stable?
cards.definition: Iron (⁵⁶Fe) and its neighbours near the peak of the curve (highest B/A)

cards.term: Why is B/A constant for 30 < A < 170?
cards.definition:
The nuclear force is short-ranged and saturating.
Each nucleon interacts only with its few neighbours, so adding nucleons does not change B/A

cards.term: What do the light-nuclei peaks at ⁴He and ¹⁶O suggest?
cards.definition: Extra stability: evidence of an atom-like shell structure in nuclei (magic numbers)

cards.term: B/A values to remember?
cards.definition: ²H ≈ 1.1, ³H ≈ 2.8, ⁴He ≈ 7.07, ¹⁶O ≈ 7.98, ⁵⁶Fe ≈ 8.79, ²³⁵U ≈ 7.6 MeV

cards.term: Why does fission of a heavy nucleus release energy?
cards.definition: Fragments (A ~ 120) have higher B/A (~8.5 MeV) than A ~ 240 (~7.6 MeV): a gain of ~0.9 MeV × 240 ≈ 216 MeV

cards.term: Why does fusion of light nuclei release energy?
cards.definition:
Fusing light nuclei gives a heavier nucleus with higher B/A, a more tightly bound (lighter) system.
The mass difference is released

cards.term: Why fission and fusion release energy
cards.definition: Both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei increase binding energy per nucleon, moving towards the peak near A = 56; the gain appears as released energy Q = Δm c²

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Binding energy per nucleon · fission and fusion

On the binding energy curve, why does splitting a heavy nucleus and joining two light nuclei both release energy?

Watch the dots climb the curve.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Binding energy per nucleon · fission and fusion

On the binding energy curve, why does splitting a heavy nucleus and joining two light nuclei both release energy?

Nuclei move up the curve toward iron (A ≈ 56, B/A ≈ 8.8 MeV): fission of A ≈ 240 (7.6 → 8.5 MeV/nucleon) gains ≈ 0.9 MeV × 240 ≈ 216 MeV; fusion of light nuclei gains even more per nucleon.

The more tightly bound the final system, the smaller its total mass; the mass difference appears as energy: Q = Δm c².

cards.term: Teacher addition: is energy released for fusion or fission per unit mass larger?
cards.definition: Fusion releases more per unit mass (about 3–4× that of fission per nucleon), e.g. D–T fusion ~ 17.6 MeV over 5 nucleons vs ~200 MeV over 236 for U fission

cards.term: Teacher addition: Q value of a nuclear reaction?
cards.definition:
\( Q = (m_i - m_f)c^2 \) with m<sub>i</sub>, m<sub>f</sub> the total initial and final rest masses
also Q = final KE − initial KE. Q > 0 exothermic (energy released)
Q < 0 endothermic (energy must be supplied)

cards.term: Features of the nuclear force: strength?
cards.definition: Much stronger than Coulomb and gravitational forces (must beat proton–proton repulsion at ~ fm distances)

cards.term: Range of the nuclear force?
cards.definition: Short range: falls rapidly to zero beyond a few femtometres, giving saturation and constant B/A

cards.term: Nuclear force between p–p, n–n and p–n?
cards.definition: Approximately the same: independent of electric charge

cards.term: Potential energy vs separation for two nucleons?
cards.definition: Minimum at r₀ ≈ 0.8 fm; attractive for r > r₀, strongly repulsive for r < r₀ (hard core)

cards.term: Is there a simple mathematical form for the nuclear force?
cards.definition: No: unlike Coulomb’s or Newton’s laws it has no simple formula

cards.term: Teacher addition: force at r = r₀ and beyond ~ 4–5 fm?
cards.definition: At r₀ the force is zero (PE minimum); beyond ~ 4–5 fm the nuclear force is negligible

cards.term: Teacher addition: the nuclear force compared with gravity in relative strength?
cards.definition: Strong : EM : weak : gravity ≈ 1 : 10⁻² : 10⁻⁶ : 10⁻³⁸

cards.term: Teacher addition: which particles mediate the nuclear force?
cards.definition: Exchange of mesons (pions) (Yukawa): the nuclear force is non-central and spin-dependent

cards.term: Who discovered radioactivity and how?
cards.definition:
Becquerel (1896):
uranium-potassium sulphate exposed to light blackened a photographic plate wrapped in black paper

cards.term: What is radioactivity?
cards.definition: A nuclear phenomenon: an unstable nucleus spontaneously decays by emitting α, β or γ radiation

cards.term: The three types of radioactive decay?
cards.definition:
α-decay: emission of ⁴₂He
β-decay: emission of electrons or positrons
γ-decay: emission of high-energy photons (100s of keV or more)

cards.term: Positron: what is it?
cards.definition: The antiparticle of the electron: same mass, equal and opposite charge (+e). An electron and positron annihilate into γ-photons

cards.term: What do α, β and γ rays consist of?
cards.definition: α: helium nuclei (charge +2e) β: electrons γ: electromagnetic radiation shorter in wavelength than X-rays

cards.term: Radioactivity as a sign of what?
cards.definition: Instability of the nucleus (neutron–proton ratio away from the stable band)

cards.term: Teacher addition: change in Z and A in α-decay?
cards.definition: Z − 2, A − 4 (parent → daughter + ⁴₂He)

cards.term: Teacher addition: change in Z and A in β⁻ and β⁺ decay?
cards.definition: β⁻: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄: Z + 1, A same. β⁺: p → n + e⁺ + ν: Z − 1, A same

cards.term: Teacher addition: change in Z and A in γ-decay?
cards.definition: None: the nucleus drops from an excited to a lower level, emitting a photon

cards.term: Teacher addition: why is a neutrino needed in β-decay?
cards.definition:
β-particles show a continuous energy spectrum.
Energy, momentum and angular momentum conservation require a third light neutral particle (neutrino/antineutrino)

cards.term: Teacher addition: penetrating power and ionising power of α, β, γ?
cards.definition: Penetration: γ > β > α (α stopped by paper). Ionisation: α > β > γ

cards.term: Teacher addition: radioactive decay law?
cards.definition:
\( N = N_0e^{-\lambda t} \)
λ = decay constant (s⁻¹)
the number decaying per second ∝ N (statistical, spontaneous, unaffected by temperature or pressure)

cards.term: Teacher addition: activity of a sample?
cards.definition: \[R = \left|\dfrac{dN}{dt}\right| = \lambda N = R_0e^{-\lambda t}\]SI unit becquerel (Bq) = 1 decay/s 1 curie = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq

cards.term: Teacher addition: half-life and mean life?
cards.definition: \[T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda},\quad \tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.44\,T_{1/2}\](τ: time to fall to 1/e)

cards.term: Teacher addition: number of nuclei left after n half-lives?
Number of nuclei left after n half-lives
cards.definition: N = N0 (1/2)^(t/T½) = N0 exp(−λt), half-life T½ = 0.693/λ; each half-life halves the remaining nuclei and the activity

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Radioactive decay · half-life

A sample has N₀ radioactive nuclei. How many are left after one, two and three half-lives?

Watch the green dots.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Radioactive decay · half-life

A sample has N₀ radioactive nuclei. How many are left after one, two and three half-lives?

Each half-life halves the number left: N = N₀ (½)t/T = N₀e−λt with T = 0.693/λ.

The pattern is statistical: which nucleus decays is random, but the fraction decaying per half-life is fixed. Activity R = λN falls in the same way.

cards.term: Teacher addition: a sample has half-life 8 days. Fraction left after 24 days? After 20 days?
cards.definition: 24 d = 3 half-lives: 1/8. 20 d = 2.5 half-lives: (½)2.5 = 0.177

cards.term: Teacher addition: half-life 5 min. Time for 87.5% to decay?
cards.definition: 12.5% = 1/8 left → 3 half-lives = 15 min

cards.term: Teacher addition: two samples with half-lives T and 2T and equal initial numbers. Ratio of initial activities?
cards.definition: R = λN: λ₁/λ₂ = 2, so R₁/R₂ = 2 : 1

cards.term: Teacher addition: does the half-life apply to a single nucleus?
cards.definition: No: it is statistical; for a single nucleus the probability of surviving one half-life is exactly ½

cards.term: Nuclear vs chemical energy per unit mass?
cards.definition:
Energy per reaction: MeV vs eV, so nuclear sources give about a million times more.
Fission of 1 kg U: ~ 10¹⁴ J
Burning 1 kg coal: ~ 10⁷ J

cards.term: Nuclear fission: definition and example?
cards.definition: A heavy nucleus splits into two intermediate-mass fragments after absorbing a neutron:\[n + {}^{235}_{92}U \to {}^{236}_{92}U \to {}^{144}_{56}Ba + {}^{89}_{36}Kr + 3n\]

cards.term: Other fission channels of ²³⁵U?
cards.definition: ¹³³₅₁Sb + ⁹⁹₄₁Nb + 4n and ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2n: on average 2–3 neutrons per fission

cards.term: Energy released per fission of a heavy nucleus?
cards.definition:
About 200 MeV (216 MeV estimated from the B/A gain of 0.9 MeV × 240).
It first appears as kinetic energy of fragments and neutrons, then as heat

cards.term: What happens to the fission fragments?
cards.definition: They are radioactive and emit β-particles in succession until they reach stable end products

cards.term: Uses of fission?
cards.definition: Controlled: nuclear reactors (electricity). Uncontrolled: atom bomb

cards.term: Teacher addition: chain reaction and multiplication factor k?
cards.definition:
Neutrons released cause further fissions.
k = neutrons produced / neutrons used
k < 1 dies out
k = 1 critical (reactor)
k > 1 explosive (bomb)

cards.term: Teacher addition: role of the moderator and the control rods in a reactor?
cards.definition:
Moderator (heavy water, graphite): slows fast neutrons to thermal energies so ²³⁵U captures them
Control rods (cadmium, boron): absorb neutrons to hold k = 1

cards.term: Teacher addition: critical mass?
cards.definition: The minimum mass of fissile material that sustains a chain reaction (neutron loss through the surface < production inside)

cards.term: Teacher addition: fissile materials?
cards.definition: ²³⁵U, ²³⁹Pu (fissile with slow neutrons); ²³⁸U is fertile (converted to ²³⁹Pu in a breeder reactor)

cards.term: Nuclear fusion: definition and energy source?
cards.definition: Two light nuclei fuse into a heavier one, releasing energy since B/A rises; it powers the Sun and all stars

cards.term: Fusion reactions in NCERT?
cards.definition: ¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν + 0.42 MeV ²H + ²H → ³He + n + 3.27 MeV ²H + ²H → ³H + ¹H + 4.03 MeV

cards.term: Why does fusion need very high temperature?
cards.definition:
The nuclei must overcome their Coulomb repulsion (barrier ~ 400 keV for two protons) so the short-range nuclear force can act.
This is thermonuclear fusion

cards.term: Estimate the temperature for proton–proton fusion.
cards.definition:
(3/2)kT ≈ 400 keV gives T ≈ 3 × 10⁹ K
The Sun’s core is only 1.5 × 10⁷ K.
Fusion happens through high-energy protons in the tail of the distribution (and tunnelling)

cards.term: Proton–proton cycle in the Sun: net reaction?
cards.definition: \[4\,{}^1_1H + 2e^- \to {}^4_2He + 2\nu + 6\gamma + 26.7\]MeV: four hydrogen atoms give one helium atom

cards.term: Steps of the p–p cycle?
cards.definition:
(i) ¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν (0.42 MeV)
(ii) e⁺ + e⁻ → γ + γ (1.02 MeV)
(iii) ²H + ¹H → ³He + γ (5.49 MeV)
(iv) ³He + ³He → ⁴He + ¹H + ¹H (12.86 MeV)

cards.term: What happens when a star exhausts core hydrogen?
cards.definition:
The core contracts and heats to ~ 10⁸ K: helium fuses to carbon.
Fusion proceeds up to elements near the iron peak of the binding-energy curve, not beyond

cards.term: Age of the Sun and its fate?
cards.definition: About 5 × 10⁹ years old with hydrogen for another 5 billion; then it swells into a red giant

cards.term: Controlled thermonuclear fusion: main challenge?
cards.definition: Fuel is a hot plasma (~10⁸ K) that no container can hold; it must be confined (magnetic confinement, e.g. tokamak; ITER). India is participating

cards.term: Teacher addition: fission vs fusion table?
cards.definition:
Fission: heavy nucleus splits, neutron-induced, chain reaction, radioactive waste, ~ 200 MeV per event
Fusion: light nuclei combine, needs 10⁷–10⁸ K, little radioactive waste, more energy per unit mass

cards.term: Teacher addition: hydrogen bomb principle?
cards.definition: Uncontrolled fusion triggered by a fission bomb that supplies the required temperature

cards.term: Mass–energy in nuclear and chemical reactions (Example 13.4)
cards.definition: Nucleon numbers conserved; binding energy differences appear as Q; chemical reactions do it too but 10⁶ times less

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 13.4 · reactions and energy

Find the missing step.

Are nuclear equations “balanced” like chemical equations? How does mass turn into energy if proton and neutron numbers are both conserved? Is mass–energy interconversion absent in chemical reactions?
  1. Chemical: atoms of each element are the same on both sides. Nuclear: elements are transmuted, but protons and neutrons (charge and baryon number) are conserved
  2. Rest masses of nucleons match on both sides; the total binding energy differs and binding energy adds a negative contribution to nuclear mass
  3. The mass difference of nuclei on the two sides is released or absorbed as energy
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 13.4 · reactions and energy

Find the missing step.

Are nuclear equations “balanced” like chemical equations? How does mass turn into energy if proton and neutron numbers are both conserved? Is mass–energy interconversion absent in chemical reactions?
  1. Chemical: atoms of each element are the same on both sides. Nuclear: elements are transmuted, but protons and neutrons (charge and baryon number) are conserved
  2. Rest masses of nucleons match on both sides; the total binding energy differs and binding energy adds a negative contribution to nuclear mass
  3. The mass difference of nuclei on the two sides is released or absorbed as energy
  4. Chemical reactions also convert mass to energy, but mass defects are ~10⁶ times smaller, so the effect is unnoticed

cards.term: Is there a separate law of conservation of mass and of energy?
cards.definition: No: a unified law of conservation of mass–energy (E = mc²)

cards.term: Which processes are exothermic on the binding-energy curve?
cards.definition: Fusion of two light nuclei and fission of a heavy nucleus into intermediate-mass nuclei

cards.term: What is the fusion condition?
cards.definition: Sufficient initial energy to overcome the Coulomb barrier (hence very high temperatures)

cards.term: Stable nuclei and the neutron–proton ratio?
cards.definition: About 1 : 1 for light nuclei rising to 3 : 2 for heavy ones; nuclei off this ratio are radioactive

cards.term: Do all fission products stay stable?
cards.definition: No: fragments are neutron-rich and undergo successive β-decays

cards.term: NEET pattern: nucleus ²³⁸₉₂U emits one α and two β⁻. Final Z and A?
cards.definition: α: Z 90, A 234; two β⁻: Z 92. Final ²³⁴₉₂U

cards.term: NEET pattern: binding energy of a nucleus is the energy…?
cards.definition: Released when the nucleus forms from free nucleons (and needed to separate it): Eb = Δm c²

cards.term: NEET pattern: nuclear density of ¹²⁵Te vs ⁶⁴Cu?
cards.definition: Equal (density independent of A). Their radii are in the ratio (125/64)1/3 = 1.25

cards.term: NEET pattern: which has higher B/A: ⁷Li or ⁵⁶Fe? Which is more stable?
cards.definition: ⁵⁶Fe (peak of the curve)

cards.term: JEE pattern: half-life 10 days; N₀ = 10⁶. Activity after 30 days relative to initially?
cards.definition: 1/8 of the initial: R = R₀/8 (three half-lives)

cards.term: JEE pattern: what fraction of the original mass converts to energy in the Sun’s p–p cycle?
cards.definition: 26.7 MeV out of 4 × 938 MeV ≈ 0.7%

cards.term: JEE pattern: energy released when one ²³⁵U undergoes fission (200 MeV): energy per gram?
cards.definition: Atoms per gram = 6.02 × 10²³/235 = 2.56 × 10²¹; × 200 MeV = 5.1 × 10²³ MeV ≈ 8.2 × 10¹⁰ J per gram

cards.term: Board pattern: differentiate nuclear fission and fusion.
cards.definition:
Fission: heavy nucleus splits (chain reaction, ~200 MeV per event, neutron induced).
Fusion: light nuclei join (needs ~ 10⁷–10⁸ K, source of stellar energy)

cards.term: Board pattern: why is nuclear density so much larger than atomic density?
cards.definition: The nucleus holds > 99.9% of the atom’s mass in ~10⁻¹² of its volume: density ~ 10¹⁷ kg/m³ vs ~10³ for ordinary matter

cards.term: Binding energy of nitrogen-14 (Exercise 13.1)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 13.1 · nitrogen-14

Find the missing step.

Binding energy of ¹⁴₇N given m(¹⁴₇N) = 14.00307 u. (Use m_H = 1.007825 u, m_n = 1.008665 u.)
  1. ΔM = 7 m_H + 7 m_n − m = 7 × 1.007825 + 7 × 1.008665 − 14.00307
  2. 7.054775 + 7.060655 − 14.00307 = 0.11236 u
  3. ?
  4. E_b ≈ 104.7 MeV (7.48 MeV per nucleon)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 13.1 · nitrogen-14

Find the missing step.

Binding energy of ¹⁴₇N given m(¹⁴₇N) = 14.00307 u. (Use m_H = 1.007825 u, m_n = 1.008665 u.)
  1. ΔM = 7 m_H + 7 m_n − m = 7 × 1.007825 + 7 × 1.008665 − 14.00307
  2. 7.054775 + 7.060655 − 14.00307 = 0.11236 u
  3. E_b = 0.11236 × 931.5 MeV
  4. E_b ≈ 104.7 MeV (7.48 MeV per nucleon)

cards.term: Exercise 13.2: binding energy of ⁵⁶Fe (55.934939 u) and ²⁰⁹Bi (208.980388 u)?
cards.definition: Fe: ΔM = 0.528461 u → 492.3 MeV, per nucleon 8.79 MeV. Bi: ΔM = 1.760877 u → 1640 MeV, per nucleon 7.85 MeV (key gives 7.84)

cards.term: Exercise 13.3: energy to separate all nucleons in a 3.0 g copper coin (⁶³Cu, 62.92960 u)?
cards.definition: ΔM per atom = 0.591935 u = 551.4 MeV atoms = (3/62.9296) × 6.023 × 10²³ = 2.87 × 10²² total 1.58 × 10²⁵ MeV = 2.5 × 10¹² J

cards.term: Exercise 13.5: Q for (i) ¹H + ³H → 2 ²H? (ii) ¹²C + ¹²C → ²⁰Ne + ⁴He?
cards.definition: (i) Q = −4.03 MeV: endothermic. (ii) Q = +4.62 MeV: exothermic

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 13.8 · lamp powered by fusion

Find the missing step.

How long can a 100 W lamp glow on the fusion of 2.0 kg of deuterium, ²H + ²H → ³He + n + 3.27 MeV?
  1. Deuterium atoms: 2000/2 × 6.023 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²⁶
  2. Each reaction uses 2 nuclei: 3.0 × 10²⁶ reactions
  3. Energy = 3.0 × 10²⁶ × 3.27 MeV = 9.85 × 10²⁶ MeV = 1.58 × 10¹⁴ J
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 13.8 · lamp powered by fusion

Find the missing step.

How long can a 100 W lamp glow on the fusion of 2.0 kg of deuterium, ²H + ²H → ³He + n + 3.27 MeV?
  1. Deuterium atoms: 2000/2 × 6.023 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²⁶
  2. Each reaction uses 2 nuclei: 3.0 × 10²⁶ reactions
  3. Energy = 3.0 × 10²⁶ × 3.27 MeV = 9.85 × 10²⁶ MeV = 1.58 × 10¹⁴ J
  4. t = E/P = 1.58 × 10¹² s ≈ 5 × 10⁴ years
